item.title: When Doomsday Predictions Steal the Future
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

When Doomsday Predictions Steal the Future

How apocalyptic fear can reshape life choices from AI to Armageddon.

Posted October 29, 2026

Key points
  • When catastrophe feels imminent, ordinary goals may seem pointless.
  • Failed prophecies can reinforce loyalty rather than trigger doubt.
  • Lifton's Aum study shows how promised salvation can justify destruction.

Over a decade ago, I interviewed former Jehovah’s Witness elder Roberto di Stefano. At the time, he had told me about a disturbing encounter that came about years after 1974, when he had delivered a congregation talk stressing to his congregants how 1975 would finally bring Armageddon.

Years later, a member approached him and described how frightened she had been. The message made her feel as though she had to sell her possessions and preach full time. She had given up so much in order to prepare for what she thought was the end.

Roberto barely remembered the talk until he found the religious bulletin and his handwritten notes. She was right. Yet when 1975 passed without Armageddon, his faith was unshaken. Perhaps, he reasoned, God was allowing more time to preach.

When we observe the results of apocalyptic belief, this is one of the core results that we see—in that a predicted world-ending event need not even arrive for the prophecy to reshape and upend someone's entire life.

Urgency Creates Obedience

This result is not at all surprising. If we are told, in no uncertain terms, that the world is ending, planning for next year or the far-away future can feel pointless. Why would anybody pursue an education, save their money, or do anything other than preach to others if none of it will even matter?

In 1974, the Watch Tower Society (Jehovah's Witnesses) had commended members selling homes and property in lieu of preaching full time. This powerful message from leadership influenced thousands of Witnesses on which life decisions to make, and which choices were praised. Members started to make irreversible decisions, such as spending their retirement savings, believing that salvation depended on acting urgently.

Since one authority claimed exclusive knowledge of the danger, the predictions had become particularly controlling. This environment ultimately led to what I call phobia indoctrination, where the ultimate authority of the group became refuge from impending catastrophe.

In such situations doubt is viewed as spiritual weakness. This continues through to today, when, for example, the recent COVID-19 pandemic was interpreted by many high-control religious groups as further proof the world was near its end.

Bringing About the End

In Destroying the World to Save It, psychiatrist Robert Jay Lifton explored an extreme example of this mindset when he studied Aum Shinrikyo, whose members, in 1995, perpetrated the Tokyo chemical gas subway attack, killing and injuring passengers.

The leader, Shoko Asahara, who claimed to be Jesus and Buddha, had taught members that such actions of destruction were part of a larger "purification." Followers were told to denounce their former lives and make decisions solely based on the guru's authority.

Lifton, examining this event, identified certain mechanisms of what he termed "ideological totalism." In Aum, he noted that "milieu control" restricted members' outside perspectives while "doctrine over person" created an environment where official teachings were more important than any individual's life.

Lifton also identified the concept of "dispensing of existence," which he described as the dividing of a population into those who deserve salvation, and those who are undeserving. Using the example of Aum's gas attack, Asahara used the idea of "purification" to tell followers that killing would save victims by allowing them to be reborn.

The actual attack pushed the group from predicting a disaster into what Lifton termed "action prophecy," where members actually moved to make the prophecy real, creating a supposed path to ultimate salvation. Such violence represents an extreme outcome, a promised future, and was the result of teachings that made human sacrifice appear virtuous and justifiable.

Language of Inevitability

Today, apocalyptic language is not confined to religion. Artificial intelligence is alternately portrayed as humanity’s inevitable destroyer or its inevitable successor.

Within the sphere of AI discussion today, there exist proponents of what researchers call effective accelerationism—or the practice of emphasizing the benefits of AI while purposefully downplaying the risks. More radical accelerationists welcome the eventual replacement of humanity by AI machines, teaching the coming of a "second race" which will explore the cosmos.

The way that religious groups position Armageddon and the way that AI accelerationists predict humanity's demise are not identical, but such rhetoric rhymes in the way that it treats humanity's fate as already set in stone. This can leave ordinary people feeling increasingly powerless as we may start to think, "Why bother investing in the future or demanding accountability if the future is decided?"

This resignation can start to infect our desire to protect the planet. For example, if the AI catastrophe is unavoidable, why bother reducing greenhouse gas emissions or worrying about the oceans?

Reclaiming Autonomy in the Future

For those who were raised in an environment that encouraged such inevitability, such as doomsday cults, predictions of AI demise can revive old fears. Such fears have indeed infected many, even those without a developmental history of being raised in a cult. And so, what can we do, when these predictions are all around us?

First, reclaiming a sense of agency starts with defining what is potential versus what is inevitable, and what is based in fear versus what can be tangibly acted on. Combating feelings of panic or helplessness requires shifting our attention to what is still ours to influence.

We can be aware of how doomsday predictions are affecting our decision making when we plan for the future and decide to pursue higher learning, maintain our health, vote, and advocate for regulation.

Living in a world where doomsday predictions create a sense of fear and uncertainty is a reality, however treating that uncertainty as a gift is a valuable interpretation. Certainty in the future means that it is a sure thing and can create a false sense of security—but uncertainty reestablishes choice and self-efficacy and removes the belief that we must postpone living for a prophecy.

item.title: 4 Ways of Not Being There
item.description:
Dissociation

4 Ways of Not Being There

Not all dissociation is the same.

Posted October 29, 2026

Key points
  • Experiences commonly called dissociation may arise from different psychological and physiological processes.
  • Research distinguishes detachment from compartmentalization, two ways to access information differently.
  • Identifying the mechanism behind an experience can help clinicians choose more appropriate interventions.

Dissociation is one of those scientific terms that has been used casually by people who have no clear understanding of what the term involves. In my practice, when they use the word and I ask them to explain the experience, I get descriptions that go from feeling numb, not remembering something, being mentally absent, or losing track of time, to experiencing their body as unfamiliar.

Some might say, “I was there, but I didn't feel anything.” Another says, “I know it happened, but I can't remember most of it.” Someone else may say they become so heavy they can't move or speak. Some mention spending hours mentally somewhere else.

What’s also interesting about this particular term is that even professionals put all those experiences in the same box: dissociation. But are they really the same thing?

Researchers have questioned this for years. More than 10 years ago, a proposition to separate dissociation into two came up, saying that there were two mechanisms easily distinguishable: detachment and compartmentalization.

Combining that proposition with my clinical observations, I add two more mechanisms that can make people feel absent or disconnected. Not all four are necessarily dissociation in the clinical sense, but they create the type of stress and fear that the term now implicitly carries when someone believes they are dissociating.

1. The Volume Is Turned Down

Source: meineresterampe/Pixabay

This first mechanism is the most popular. it includes a woman describing her father's death as casually as talking about the weather, a man who feels as if watching himself arguing with his wife from a foot away, or someone who looks at his street as if it was a movie set after a heavy day at work.

These experiences are dissociative and easily recognizable clinically as emotional numbing, depersonalization, and derealization. The mechanism they share is a change in how emotions, the self, or surroundings are experienced. It’s a temporary distancing that can be useful in some situations, like when a parent needs to remain composed while taking an injured child to the hospital. The problem here, and in almost every other dissociative experience, comes when the mechanism doesn’t stop and the experience becomes chronic.

I like describing this type as if the volume of the experience has been turned down. Volume down makes the heavy experience less loud. The brain uses this mechanism because it assumes the full volume of the emotional response may be unbearable.

This has been investigated. Neuroimaging research has found that some trauma-related dissociative experiences involve a higher-than-ordinary regulation of emotional responses that reduce the awareness of the reaction. It’s been proposed as the most probable mechanism even when it may not apply to every experience we call detachment.

2. The Connection Is Missing

Source: Pixabay

The other recognized type of dissociation is called compartmentalization.

The experiences here are better identified than the mechanisms behind them. Think of someone not remembering writing the texts they sent, or someone who recalls a childhood experience when talking to their brother but goes blank if the issue is brought up by the parents. This mechanism works similar to a working lamp that isn't plugged in. The capacity may be there but it won’t light up because that access has been interrupted.

This type of dissociation is probably the most severe issue because it involves discontinuities in memory, as in dissociative amnesia, or identity, as in dissociative identity disorder.

An accepted theory is that repeated overwhelming experiences, especially during childhood, may influence how memory, awareness, and identity develop, and that some connections may have developed without linking to each other, which creates that sense of fragmentation or absence that may be feel so disempowering.

3. The Whole System Shifts

Source: Pixabay

There is another response, commonly called shutdown, whose place within dissociation remains controversial. Some researchers consider it a related defensive response rather than dissociation itself but many people think of it as the epitome of dissociation and trauma. It often occurs during overwhelming stress, particularly when a threat seems inescapable. Imagine someone receiving devastating news. Their system reacts in such a way that the body becomes heavy, thinking slows down, and moving or speaking becomes difficult, sometimes to the point of immobility.

It’s different than numbing because someone who is emotionally numb is still responsive. In shutdown, however, the person's overall physiological state changes, affecting energy, movement, and the capacity to act. If numbing is low volume, shutdown is like a phone entering battery-saver mode. Other dissociative experiences, such as emotional detachment, may occur at the same time, but that doesn't make them the same mechanism.

Shutdown is generally a temporary defensive response that subsides as the system recovers. However, in some people, similar responses may be activated repeatedly, sometimes by situations that no longer present the original level of threat.

4. Attention Goes Elsewhere

Source: Pixabay

Another experience frequently included in dissociative descriptions involves absorption, although researchers disagree about where it belongs.

Think about becoming so absorbed in a novel that you don't hear someone calling your name, or driving home with little recollection of the journey. Attention has concentrated elsewhere, like a radio tuned to another station.

But it can also look like someone spending hours creating elaborate imaginary worlds, complete with characters, relationships, and conflicts. Even when they generally recognize these worlds as imaginary, returning to ordinary life may become increasingly difficult. This is sometimes called maladaptive daydreaming that is assumed to be pathological and dysfunctional.

Absorption, like other dissociative manifestations, isn't necessarily pathological. It's a normal attentional capacity that can become problematic only when it becomes difficult to regulate. That's why I think attention deserves a place in this conversation, even if some forms of absorption don't qualify as dissociation.

Why the Difference Matters

In general, dissociative experiences feel strange and many times frightening, but many are temporary and harmless. I think that understanding the mechanism could help us decide what might help:

  • When the volume is turned down, treatment may involve gradually restoring access to emotional experience.
  • When connections are missing, the work may focus on improving access and continuity between experiences or states.
  • When the whole system shifts, we need to find what triggers that response and help restore the capacity to act.
  • When attention repeatedly goes elsewhere, we might ask what the inner world provides that ordinary life doesn't.

Each needs a different starting point.

Knowing which process is operating helps us understand what's happening, why it persists, and what might help us become more fully present again.

item.title: Why Doesn't Happiness Last?
item.description:
Happiness

Why Doesn't Happiness Last?

Why pain lingers and contentment fades.

Posted October 29, 2026

Key points
  • The brain is wired for caution over comfort.
  • Savoring offsets fading happiness.
  • Appreciating the present can help bring contentment.

Why doesn’t happiness last?

A patient asked me this question in a session the other day.

My answer? We’re actually wired that way.

Our brains are neurobiologically designed to notice negative or dangerous things first. It’s what kept our ancestors alive and enabled us to survive as a species. When something new or wonderful happens, whether it’s a wave of joy, excitement, or pure happiness, those feelings naturally fade over time as we get used to our new reality. Psychologists call this hedonic adaptation. The good news is that we can actually teach ourselves to savor positive experiences and stretch out those good feelings a bit longer. Now, this isn't about erasing the negative, because let's be honest, that’s not realistic. Instead, it’s about training our minds to notice, appreciate, and linger on what’s good.

The Brain’s Safety-First Mindset

At its core, your brain has one primary job, which is to keep you safe. Because of that, detecting potential threats will always rank higher on your internal radar than taking in a pleasant moment. Your brain's threat-detection system relies heavily on two key players—the amygdala, which scans for danger, and the hippocampus, which stores and pulls up memories to give those threats context. Together with other brain structures, they keep you on alert so you’re not caught off guard.

Picture yourself driving in heavy, bumper-to-bumper traffic. Your brain goes straight into survival mode, focusing on the car cutting into your lane, watching taillights, and calculating how fast you need to brake. In that moment, you won't even notice the colorful sunset, the dramatic autumn clouds, or the smell of crisp fall leaves outside your open window. Your brain simply triaged those sensory experiences as non-essential to your immediate survival.

And it’s not just our neuroanatomy that pulls us toward the dark side. How we think does that as well. Research shows we naturally give far more cognitive and emotional weight to negative events, criticism, or perceived risks than to positive ones of equal size. This is called the negativity bias.

What This Means for Living With Depression

For anyone living with depression, this negativity bias can feel like it’s turned up to maximum volume. Depression often brings anhedonia—the heavy, frustrating loss of the ability to feel pleasure—along with low mood, distress, or self-criticism. When you’re depressed, positive moments don’t just fade quickly; sometimes they feel almost impossible to register at all. When you're in that space, you often have to work hard to find them. Sometimes you have to intentionally create them. And when you do find them, savoring shouldn't be about forcing fake positivity or pretending everything’s fine. It’s about letting yourself lean into brief moments of ease.

Directing your focus to these small, pleasant moments may feel hard at first. But with time and practice, you can use savoring as a skill set to bring you contentment. By doing so, you gently remind your brain, your thoughts, and your emotions to welcome something good. And research says this can enhance well-being.

Offsetting the Negative

Slowing down to really feel a positive moment can soften your natural urge towards hypervigilance. While hedonic adaptation will always make happiness fade over time, here are five ways to invite more contentment into your day.

  1. Take five. Give yourself just five minutes to fully sink into a pleasant moment. It could be watching the sunset, sipping a hot drink, or acknowledging a small task you finished today. Notice how your body feels. What do your senses pick up? Does it bring a smile or a feeling of warmth? Resist the urge to rush straight to the next thing on your to-do list.
  2. Get Comfortable With Ordinary Moments. Learn to appreciate simple, unplanned moments. Focus on slowing down and building tolerance for quiet, unexciting downtime without feeling the urge to fill it with something more.
  3. Feed Your Senses Daily. Invite sensory moments into your day with total intention. Look at the colors you see outside your window, delight in the aroma of your meal cooking, the cozy feel of a favorite sweater, or the sound of the rhythm of rain outside. Engaging your physical senses roots you directly in the present.
  4. Redefine Contentment. Remember that contentment isn't meant to be a nonstop high or a rush of ecstasy. It’s simply a calm state of ease. When we stop expecting contentment to feel like a thrill, it becomes much easier to spot—and hold on to.
  5. Practice Daily Self-Acceptance. Before you go to sleep, find one thing that went well during your day. Instead of just making a quick acknowledgment of it, linger for a moment on why what happened went well and how it made you feel. Honor the moment and accept it within yourself as a good thing.

It’s true that happiness doesn’t last forever. Neurobiologically speaking, it was never designed to. But while we can’t stop positive feelings from fading, we can create more moments of contentment simply by making time for short, intentional savoring moments. Finding true peace doesn’t come from trying to make happiness stay unchanged. Finding well-being starts when we learn to appreciate what’s good right now, without demanding that it linger forever. When we allow ourselves to live in the margins of simple, everyday moments, we give ourselves permission to experience a sense of ease one small breath at a time.
